summary: Introduces the revised Internationalized Domain Names for Applications (IDNA) protocol, which lets domain names contain characters from many scripts. This document describes the set of documents that make up the revision and supplies definitions common to all of them. It is a Proposed Standard and replaced RFC 3490.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5890 defines the terms used by IDNA2008, a system for using international characters in domain names. It explains how Unicode labels correspond to ASCII labels that DNS can carry.

questions: what is an a-label and a u-label
what does xn-- mean in a domain name
subtitle: The shared definitions behind the revised internationalized domain-name system.

tldr.problem: Domain names need a consistent way to represent labels written with characters beyond ASCII while remaining usable in DNS.
tldr.mechanism: IDNA2008 defines label categories and conversion between Unicode U-labels and ASCII A-labels, and organizes the documents that specify the rules.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5890 supplies definitions for IDNA2008 and obsoletes RFC 3490; the protocol and character rules are specified in companion RFCs.

today: RFC 5890 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3490. It provides shared definitions for IDNA2008; RFC 5891 specifies the core protocol.

sections.title: A Framework for IDNA2008
sections.content:
Internationalized Domain Names for Applications (IDNA) lets applications handle domain-name labels containing characters beyond ASCII. RFC 5890 is the definitions document in the IDNA2008 set; it does not specify the whole protocol by itself.

The set also includes protocol rules, rules for right-to-left labels, permitted-character tables, and rationale. RFC 5890 describes how these documents fit together and defines terms they share.
sections.plainLanguage: IDNA2008 is a set of related specifications for domain names with international characters. This RFC is the shared glossary and guide to that set.

sections.title: Labels, A-Labels, and U-Labels
sections.content:
A domain name is made of labels separated by dots. An A-label is the ASCII-compatible form of an IDNA-valid label and begins with the prefix xn--; a U-label is the corresponding valid Unicode form.

A U-label must be in Unicode Normalization Form C and include at least one non-ASCII character. A-label and U-label forms must convert to each other consistently. Ordinary ASCII labels that meet the LDH rules are called NR-LDH labels; IDNA-aware applications use A-labels, U-labels, and NR-LDH labels.
sections.plainLanguage: A U-label is the Unicode spelling of an internationalized domain-name label. Its A-label is the ASCII form used for DNS, usually recognizable by the xn-- prefix.

sections.title: How the Two Label Forms Relate
sections.content:
IDNA works on complete labels rather than on pieces of a domain name. Punycode converts between a U-label and its A-label by adding or removing the ASCII-Compatible Encoding prefix.

Both forms must meet the DNS label rules and IDNA validity requirements. A label that merely starts with xn-- is not necessarily a valid A-label: its remainder must be valid Punycode output and decode to a valid U-label.
sections.plainLanguage: IDNA converts one whole label at a time. The xn-- prefix alone does not prove that the label is valid; the encoded text must pass the IDNA checks.

sections.title: Which Labels Are Valid and Equivalent
sections.content:
An IDNA-aware application accepts A-labels, U-labels, and NR-LDH labels in the contexts defined by the protocol. Reserved LDH labels that are not A-labels are not valid IDNA labels. An internationalized domain name contains at least one A-label or U-label and may mix those with NR-LDH labels.

Two labels are equivalent when their A-label forms match using DNS case-insensitive comparison. The specification does not require a general mapping from one Unicode string to another before comparison.
sections.plainLanguage: Only specific label forms count as valid IDNA labels. To compare two forms, convert them to A-labels and compare those without regard to ASCII letter case.

sections.title: Security and Application Limits
sections.content:
Different interpretations of an internationalized name can lead users to different servers. The RFC calls out visually similar characters, differing local character-set conversions, and legacy names as risks; it suggests showing users when a name mixes scripts but notes that no complete technical solution exists.

A Unicode U-label can be much longer than its encoded A-label and may reach 252 characters. Applications should allow for that difference and guard against truncation or buffer errors.
sections.plainLanguage: Names that look alike may still point to different places, so software should help users notice potentially confusing labels. Applications also need to handle Unicode labels that are longer than their DNS-encoded forms.
